name: Anong
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sun Hongkai. 1988. Notes on Anong, a new language (transl. Li Fengxiang). Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 11(1): 27-63. DOI 10.15144/LTBA-11.1.27. Open scan:https://sealang.net/sala/archives/pdf8/sun1988notes.pdf
catalog_locator: p. 33 (scan page 7 of 37), sections 'III. Tones' and 'IV. Syllables'
catalog_quote: There are four tones: high level 55, high falling 53, low falling 31, and high rising 35. There is also an unstable mid-level tone which becomes a high-level tone when influenced by low-falling and high-rising tones, and becomes a low-falling tone when influenced by high-falling and high-level tones. Thus, in my description this mid-level tone has been treated as an environmentally-conditioned variant of other tones. The high-level and low-falling tones have a higher frequency than the other two tones. Tones carry a low functional load in terms of differentiating meaning. ... A syllable is usually composed of an initial, a final, and a tone, although some syllables consist of a final and a tone without an initial. Syllables consist of from one to five phonemes. The syllable canon is illustrated below, using C for consonant, and V for vowel; all the syllables have a tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Anong is described as a four-tone language (55, 53, 31, 35, with a conditioned mid tone) in which every syllable carries a tone; the sketch says nothing about word stress or accent at all, so no stress rule can be extracted. The only hint of prominence asymmetry is that prefixes are called 'reduced syllables' with simple vowels and no finals (p. 36).
new_statements.exceptions: Tones have low functional load; unstable mid tone is treated as an allotone.
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable/word level; citation forms from the Mugujia Township, Fugong County (Yunnan) variety as recorded by Sun in 1960s-80s.
new_statements.identity_note: Sun 1988 describes Anong as spoken in Mugujia Township, Fugong County, Nujiang, Yunnan (the Chinese side; Glottolog nung1282 'Nung (Myanmar)' = Anong/Anung [nun], countries CN;MM). The Myanmar variety (Khwingsang/Kwingsang) is not described in any opened source; Shintani 2018 covers it. No separate glottocode for the Myanmar dialect.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Thurgood 2010, printed p. 57 (PDF page 18), section 3.2: 'all of the following developments are found in other Tibeto-Burman languages: a prefixal sɯ³¹- losing its unstressed vowel, fusing with the following root, devoicing a root initial stop or nasal, and then dropping.' A passing note that the Anong causative prefix vowel is unstressed (root carries the prominence); not a statement of a word-stress system and it does not change the reading. No stress statement of any kind in Wu 2013.

tone_statements.citation: Thurgood, Ela. 2011. Tonal variations in Anong. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 129(4_Supplement): 2451 (161st ASA Meeting abstract).
tone_statements.quote: Anong citation tones are characterized by three features. First, the tonal space is small. Second, onset consonant type correlates with the pitch height of the following vowel. Third, non-modal phonation is not an acoustic cue to any of the five tones. Neither is it a contrastive property of vowels. In disyllabic utterances, the F0 shapes and heights on the first-syllable tones can be readily related to the F0 shapes and heights in the citation forms. The F0 value of the second-syllable tones depends on the offset value of the tone in the first syllable. However, disyllabic forms with the prefix /a31/ follow a different pattern, one in which the first-syllable tone is raised.
tone_statements.locator: abstract, JASA 129(4_Supplement) p. 2451 (text as given in the Crossref record for DOI 10.1121/1.3588044)

sources.note: Acoustic analysis of Anong citation tones and tones in disyllables; FIVE tones; small tonal space; onset consonant type correlates with pitch height; non-modal phonation is not a cue to any tone nor contrastive on vowels; second-syllable F0 depends on first-syllable tone offset; prefix a31- forms raise the first-syllable tone (with laryngealization/duration). Note: five tones vs the four (+unstable mid) of Sun 1988 listed here — consistent with the later-described 33 tone (Sun & Liu 2009), not a contradiction of tonality.
